name: Aaron Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the corrugator at Greaves Packaging, the cardboard box plant by the railway. The corrugator is a long machine, about as long as a football pitch, that glues paper into cardboard sheets. I'm the junior at the dry end, so I stack sheets, check the board isn't warped and shout when the glue's off. Twelve months in, and the operator, Big Tony, still won't let me touch the controls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew, it's like a football team, everyone has a position. I coach the under-tens at the parish club on Saturdays, so I'm used to that. What wears me out is the heat off the steam rolls and the money. My fiancée Gina works on reception at a dental practice, and we're saving for a wedding next summer on almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can all stop panicking and get on with the job. At work I'd say hard work still counts. I'd maybe share a joke about it in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for the plant, boxes always need making. But our money's still tight, under a month saved, and the wedding's costing more than we thought. Greaves is the only big employer this side of town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and ask Big Tony to start teaching me the controls. I'd do Saturday overtime instead of a second coaching session, though I'd hate that. And we'd cut the wedding guest list a bit, sorry Auntie Rosa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, but the money nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gina's mum, mostly, she's got opinions. The chatbot made us a wedding budget sheet, and it says we're two thousand short. We'd cut the band and get my cousin to do a playlist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding mean to you, beyond the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the start of a family, and I want to do it right, in church, with both families there. My parents did it on nothing and they're still together. That counts for more than the band.

say: I'd say we can **stop panicking** and get on with the job.
I'd tell the crew that **hard work** still counts.
think: Boxes always need making, so **Greaves** is fine for now.
Our **money is tight**, under a month saved, with the wedding coming.
do: Ask Big Tony to start teaching me the **corrugator controls**.
Do **Saturday overtime** instead of a second coaching session.
Cut the **wedding guest list** and replace the band with a playlist.
feel: He feels **mostly fine** about the job.
S0.quote: The chatbot made us a wedding budget sheet, and it says we're two thousand short.
fieldNote: His job feels safe but **wedding costs** and thin savings press on him.

**Family and church** frame what he cares about.

steps.text: Ask the corrugator operator to teach him the controls
Work Saturday overtime at Greaves instead of a second coaching session
Cut the wedding band and some guests to close the two-thousand gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change, and we'll adapt like we always have. At work I'd tell the lads to keep their heads. At the football club I'd tell the parents to make sure the kids learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Gina than me. Answering phones and booking appointments is exactly what the card says goes first. If my fiancée's dental practice puts in an AI receptionist, we're down to one wage just before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what Greaves does with the new tech, then learn whatever they bring in. I'd tell Gina to start asking about dental nurse training, because that's hands-on. And we'd push the wedding back a few months if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my job, for our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Gina take that advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it at first, she likes the front desk and chatting to patients. But she's sensible. Her sister's a dental nurse, so she knows the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the government for help if Gina lost her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather lean on family first. My parents and Gina's would help us out for a few months. I don't like the idea of handouts when I'm young and able.

I'd tell football parents to make sure kids learn a **trade**.
think: I'm more worried about **Gina's** reception job than mine.

Push the **wedding** back a few months if needed.
feel: He feels **anxious** for their plans, not his job.

fieldNote: His worry shifts to his **fiancée's job**, which is thinking work.
A household earner's risk makes him **anxious**, though his own job looks safe.

steps.text: Wait to see what tech Greaves brings in, then learn it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families first, and businesses should keep people on as long as they can. At church I'd say we stick together. I wouldn't post much, it'd just be panic online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Gina's job goes in 2028 and mine goes around 2031. Greaves would put robots on the dry end the minute they're cheap. We'd be newly married with no jobs and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Gina anyway, but small, in the parish hall. I'd ask Greaves to train me on maintenance, because someone needs to look after the robots. And I'd look at the army, my uncle did it and they teach you a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd keep me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The army is a big step. What makes you think of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Paolo did twelve years in the army engineers and came out a qualified electrician. It's steady pay, a roof, and a trade. Gina wouldn't love it, but I'd do it if Greaves shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the under-tens' parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to teach their kids to work with their hands and be good people. I don't know what jobs will be there. But I know good people get looked after.

say: I'd say we must look after **families first** and keep people on.
I'd say at church that we **stick together**.
think: Gina's job goes in **2028** and mine around **2031**.
We'd be newly married with **no jobs** and no savings.
do: Marry Gina **small**, in the parish hall.
Look into joining the **army engineers** for a trade.
S2.quote: My uncle Paolo did twelve years in the army engineers and came out a qualified electrician.
fieldNote: He reads the **3-year gap** between Gina's job and his.
The **army** is a serious backup, from his uncle's example.
Faith and family stay central; the **wedding** goes ahead small.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding in the parish hall
Ask Greaves for robot maintenance training
Talk to an army recruiter about the engineers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people get on with it. At work I'd say get a ticket, a proper qualification. At church I'd say look out for each other's kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me get a maintenance qualification before the robots come in 2034. Gina has time to move into dental nursing before 2031. It's tight, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Greaves to sponsor an engineering apprenticeship, they've done it for two lads before. Gina would start the nursing course this year. We'd have the wedding next summer as planned, but cheaper, and save fifty a month after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Greaves says no to the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the college at night and pay it myself, somehow. Maybe my dad would help. My dad always said a trade is worth more than a house. I'd pay him back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want children soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait till Gina's qualified and I've got the ticket. Maybe 2030. I'd want our kids to have steady parents.

I'd tell coworkers to get a **proper qualification**.
think: I can get a **maintenance qualification** before robots arrive in 2034.

do: Ask Greaves to sponsor an **engineering apprenticeship**.
Support Gina starting the **nursing course** this year.
Hold the wedding cheaper and save **fifty a month** after.
feel: He feels **worried**, but a plan helps.
S3.quote: My dad always said a trade is worth more than a house.
fieldNote: He plans **two careers** around the 2031 and 2034 dates.

steps.text: Ask Greaves to sponsor an engineering apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so no one has an excuse. At work I'd say get trained while you can. At the club I'd tell parents to think about trades for their kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots do. By then I'd want to be a qualified engineer with a family, and Gina settled as a dental nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the engineering apprenticeship over the next three or four years. We'd have the wedding as planned, maybe a child around 2029. And I'd save a bit for a deposit on a small house near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier, but I'd still keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd keep it, church and everyone. Ten years is enough to get married properly and still plan. Auntie Rosa can come after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens after 2039. The kids I coach will be in their twenties right when the robots arrive. I'd want them to have something.

I'd tell parents to think about **trades** for their kids.
think: By 40 I want to be a **qualified engineer** with a family.
do: Complete an **engineering apprenticeship** over three or four years.
Have the **wedding** as planned and a child around 2029.
Save for a **house deposit** near my parents.
S4.quote: The kids I coach will be in their twenties right when the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep **family plans** intact.
His worry shifts to the **under-tens** he coaches.

steps.text: Complete an engineering apprenticeship within four years
Hold the church wedding and plan a child around 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Gina and I would lose work just as we started married life. What would help is firms paying for apprenticeships, and families and churches pulling together. A hand up, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. I coach under-tens, and I want them to have a trade to aim for. If the robots take the trades too, what do we tell them?
